spark.summary: The Gang of Four (GoF) patterns—especially Strategy, Decorator, Factory, and Observer—provide battle-tested structural templates for swapping algorithms, layering cross-cutting behavior, encapsulating object creation, and decoupling event producers from consumers.
spark.keyTakeaway: Reach for patterns to isolate a concrete axis of change (varying pricing rules, composable I/O streams, multi-channel alerts), never as preemptive ceremony around static code.

concept.whyItMatters: Without these four patterns, teams either copy-paste `if/else` chains across every billing and routing module or hardcode cross-cutting concerns (retries, metrics, auth) directly into business classes—making every new feature a risky edit to core code.
whenToUse: Strategy: Multiple interchangeable algorithms exist for one task (e.g., Stripe vs. UPI vs. NetBanking fee calculation, or BM25 vs. vector reranking) selected at runtime.
Decorator: You need to dynamically stack orthogonal behaviors (compression, buffering, rate limiting, circuit breaking) around a core interface without subclass explosion.
Factory / Observer: Creation involves complex conditional setup or resource pooling (Factory), or one domain event must fan out to independent downstream listeners without coupling (Observer).
whenNotToUse: A simple `if/else` or `switch` has only 2 stable branches that rarely change—creating 4 interface files adds indirection for zero gain.
Modern language features already solve the problem cleanly: Python first-class functions/lambdas or Java `Function<T, R>` often replace single-method Strategy classes.
Distributed cross-service messaging where reliable delivery, retries, and backpressure are required—use Kafka/SQS rather than an in-process Observer list.
keyPoints: Strategy encapsulates a family of algorithms behind a shared interface so the host context delegates work without branching on type.
Decorator wraps an object implementing the same interface (`BufferedInputStream(GZIPInputStream(FileInputStream))`), enabling O(N) composable wrappers instead of O(2^N) subclasses.
Factory Method / Abstract Factory centralizes instantiation logic, hiding concrete classes, validation, and object reuse behind a clean creation boundary.
Observer defines a one-to-many publish-subscribe contract inside a process so state changes notify registered listeners without the subject knowing their concrete types.
All four patterns favor object composition over deep inheritance hierarchies, keeping classes small and open for extension.

examples.title: Composable HTTP Client Middleware via Decorator
examples.scenario: A Java microservice calls external partner APIs and needs configurable timeouts, exponential-backoff retries, Prometheus latency metrics, and bearer-token injection.
examples.outcome: Wrapping `HttpClient` in `RetryingClient(MetricsClient(AuthClient(OkHttpTransport)))` lets each concern be unit-tested in isolation and toggled per partner without touching transport code.

examples.title: Dynamic Freight & Surge Pricing via Strategy + Factory
examples.scenario: A logistics platform calculates delivery quotes differently for Standard, Express, Cold-Chain, and Rain-Surge orders across cities.
examples.outcome: A `PricingStrategyFactory` maps `(tier, city)` to a `PricingStrategy` bean (`ExpressPricingStrategy`, etc.). Adding a new festive-surge rule takes one new class and zero edits to `QuoteService`.

tradeOffs.pro: New behaviors (e.g., a new Strategy or Decorator) are added as isolated files with zero risk of breaking existing branches.
tradeOffs.con: Jumping through 4 layers of interfaces and wrappers makes stack traces deeper and IDE 'Go to Implementation' harder for newcomers.

tradeOffs.factor: In-Process Observer vs. Explicit Orchestration / Message Queue
tradeOffs.pro: Zero infrastructure overhead and instant decoupling for UI events or local cache invalidation.
tradeOffs.con: Execution order is often implicit, slow observers block the publisher thread unless async, and exceptions in one listener can abort others.

tradeOffs.pro: Prevents combinatorial class explosion (`EncryptedCompressedBufferedStream`) by composing wrappers at runtime.
tradeOffs.con: Wrapper ordering bugs (e.g., compressing *after* encrypting destroys compression ratio) are not caught by the type system.

failureModes.name: Lapsed Listener Memory Leak (Observer)
failureModes.description: Short-lived UI components or per-request handlers subscribe to a long-lived singleton Subject and never unsubscribe, pinning them in heap until OOM.
failureModes.mitigation: Use explicit `AutoCloseable` subscription tokens, `WeakReference` listener registries, or structured lifecycle hooks that unregister on teardown.

failureModes.name: Decorator Ordering Bug
failureModes.description: Wrapping `GzipDecorator(EncryptDecorator(stream))` encrypts data first (turning it into high-entropy noise), making Gzip inflate size instead of shrinking it.
failureModes.mitigation: Expose a Builder or Factory that enforces canonical wrapper ordering (`Encrypt -> Compress -> Buffer`) rather than letting callers stack decorators arbitrarily.

failureModes.name: Pattern Over-Engineering (Strategy for 1 Implementation)
failureModes.description: Teams wrap every helper in `AbstractXFactory` + `XStrategy` + `DefaultXStrategyImpl` 'just in case', tripling file count.
failureModes.mitigation: Follow the Rule of Three: write direct code first, and extract Strategy/Factory only when a second or third genuine variant arrives.

failureModes.name: Synchronous Observer Cascade Failure
failureModes.description: A slow analytics listener in an in-memory `OrderCreated` Observer loop takes 3 seconds per event, stalling checkout latency.
failureModes.mitigation: Isolate non-critical observers onto bounded async executors with timeouts and exception boundaries, or move them to an outbox/Kafka topic.

commonMistakes: Confusing Decorator (same interface, adds behavior) with Adapter (converts incompatible interface A to B) or Proxy (controls access/lazy-loading).
Using heavy Strategy classes in Python or Java 17+ when a `dict[str, Callable]` or `Enum` with a lambda/method is cleaner.
Allowing a Factory to return `null` on unknown keys instead of throwing an explicit `IllegalArgumentException` or returning an `Optional`.
Mutating shared state inside a singleton Strategy instance, causing race conditions across concurrent requests.
Letting Observers mutate the Subject during notification, triggering infinite feedback loops.

sections.content:
## The idea

The 1994 *Design Patterns* (Gang of Four) catalog named recurring object-oriented solutions to change management. Rather than hardcoding *how* an operation runs, *what* concrete class is built, or *who* reacts to state changes, these four core patterns introduce **polymorphic seams**: **Factory** isolates creation, **Strategy** isolates algorithmic variation, **Decorator** isolates composable cross-cutting layers, and **Observer** isolates event fan-out. Used together, they keep core domain workflows stable while surrounding requirements evolve.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an order-notification pipeline in Java:

1. **Factory**: `NotifierFactory.forChannel(Channel.WHATSAPP)` inspects config and returns a `WhatsAppNotifier` without `AlertService` importing Twilio/Meta SDKs.
2. **Decorator**: The factory wraps the raw sender: `new RateLimitedNotifier(new RetryingNotifier(new WhatsAppNotifier(client), 3), bucket)`. Each layer implements `Notifier.send(Message)`.
3. **Strategy**: `MessageFormatter` is a Strategy (`CompactSmsFormatter` vs. `RichWhatsAppFormatter`) injected into the notifier to render payloads per channel.
4. **Observer**: When `PaymentService` marks an invoice `PAID`, it publishes `InvoicePaidEvent` to registered `EventListener` observers (`AlertService`, `AuditLogListener`, `AnalyticsListener`), keeping `PaymentService` completely unaware of notifications.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Modern language idioms vs. classic GoF
sections.content:
## Modern language idioms vs. classic GoF

Classic GoF was written in 1994 for C++ and Smalltalk, where functions were not first-class values. Today:

- **Strategy**: In Python, a `dict[str, Callable[[Order], Decimal]]` or `Protocol` replaces 5 boilerplate subclasses. In Java 21, `sealed interface` + `switch` pattern matching handles closed algorithm sets concisely, while `Function<T, R>` covers single-method strategies.
- **Decorator**: Python's `@retry(max_attempts=3)` syntax is built-in function decoration, whereas Java still uses explicit interface wrappers (`FilterInputStream`) or Spring AOP.
- **Factory**: Static factory methods (`List.of()`, `Duration.ofSeconds()`) often replace full `AbstractFactory` hierarchies unless families of related products must vary together.

## Pattern selection matrix

| Pattern | Core Intent | Real-World Stdlib / Framework Example | Primary Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Strategy** | Swap algorithms at runtime via shared interface | `java.util.Comparator<T>` in `List.sort()` | Overkill when a 2-branch `if` or lambda suffices |
| **Decorator** | Stack behaviors dynamically without subclassing | `new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in))` | Wrapper order bugs (e.g., compress vs. encrypt) |
| **Factory** | Encapsulate complex creation & concrete type selection | `DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance()`, `LoggerFactory` | Unnecessary `AbstractFactory` bloat for simple POJOs |
| **Observer** | Decouple 1-to-many in-process event notifications | Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher`, DOM `addEventListener` | Lapsed-listener memory leaks & blocking publisher threads |

## Failure modes

- **Infinite Notification Cycles (Observer)**: Listener A updates Property X, which triggers Listener B, which updates Property Y, which triggers Listener A. Guard with idempotency checks (`if (newVal.equals(oldVal)) return;`).
- **Opaque Debugging in Deep Decorator Chains**: A 7-layer decorator stack produces 40-frame stack traces and hides which layer swallowed an exception. Keep stacks <=3–4 layers and log layer names on failure.
- **Factory Switch-Statement Rot**: A central `switch (type)` factory grows to 300 lines and violates Open/Closed. Use a self-registering map (`Map<String, Supplier<Strategy>>` or Spring `List<Strategy>` injection).
- **Stateful Strategy Race Conditions**: Storing per-request fields on a singleton Strategy bean causes cross-request data corruption under concurrency.

## Combining patterns cleanly

Patterns rarely live alone—they compose naturally when each owns one boundary. A **Factory** is the ideal place to enforce **Decorator** ordering so callers never accidentally swap retry and circuit-breaker layers. Similarly, **Strategy** objects should remain stateless so a **Factory** can safely cache and reuse them as flyweights. When **Observer** notifications need guaranteed delivery across restarts, replace the in-memory listener list with the Transactional Outbox pattern backed by Kafka or SQS.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify at least 2–3 concrete variations exist before introducing a Strategy or Factory.
- [ ] Keep Strategy implementations stateless so they are safe as singletons.
- [ ] Enclose Decorator assembly inside a Builder or Factory to guarantee correct layer ordering.
- [ ] Always provide an `unsubscribe()` / `AutoCloseable` handle for every Observer registration.
- [ ] Prefer language-native lambdas/functions over single-method Strategy boilerplate where idiomatic.

interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are leading the design of a distributed application encountering bottlenecks in Software Design & Architecture. How do you leverage GoF Design Patterns: Strategy, Decorator, Factory & Observer to guarantee high availability?

dimensions.name: Pattern Selection & Execution
dimensions.description: Applying GoF Design Patterns: Strategy, Decorator, Factory & Observer effectively.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Deploy GoF Design Patterns: Strategy, Decorator, Factory & Observer with strict monitoring thresholds and graceful degradation fallbacks.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: The Gang of Four (GoF) patterns—especially Strategy, Decorator, Factory, and Observer—provide battle-tested structural templates for swapping algorithms, layering cross-cutting behavior, encapsulating object creation, and decoupling event producers from consumers.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Retry -> RateLimit -> Sender applies the primary invariant and coordinates with MessageFormatter.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, MessageFormatter experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use explicit `AutoCloseable` subscription tokens, `WeakReference` listener registries, or structured lifecycle hooks that unregister on teardown.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Reach for patterns to isolate a concrete axis of change (varying pricing rules, composable I/O streams, multi-channel alerts), never as preemptive ceremony around static code.
Avoid trap: Confusing Decorator (same interface, adds behavior) with Adapter (converts incompatible interface A to B) or Proxy (controls access/lazy-loading).
Avoid trap: Using heavy Strategy classes in Python or Java 17+ when a `dict[str, Callable]` or `Enum` with a lambda/method is cleaner.
When to reach for it: Strategy: Multiple interchangeable algorithms exist for one task (e.g., Stripe vs. UPI vs. NetBanking fee calculation, or BM25 vs. vector reranking) selected at runtime.
When to reach for it: Decorator: You need to dynamically stack orthogonal behaviors (compression, buffering, rate limiting, circuit breaking) around a core interface without subclass explosion.

putItTogether.title: Putting Design Patterns Gof Together
putItTogether.summary: Reach for patterns to isolate a concrete axis of change (varying pricing rules, composable I/O streams, multi-channel alerts), never as preemptive ceremony around static code.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Design Patterns Gof before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Wrapping `HttpClient` in `RetryingClient(MetricsClient(AuthClient(OkHttpTransport)))` lets each concern be unit-tested in isolation and toggled per partner without touching transport code.
